meaning: The one infinite reality: existence, consciousness and fullness, without a second.
The Self: pure witnessing consciousness, which Advaita holds to be identical with Brahman.
The inexplicable power by which the one reality appears as the many; neither real nor simply unreal.
Ignorance of one's true nature; the root cause of bondage, removed only by knowledge.
Ignorance: a near synonym of avidyā, the not-knowing of the Self that Advaita holds to be the root of bondage.
Superimposition: taking one thing for another, as a rope for a snake, or the body for the Self.
Knowledge; in Advaita, the direct knowledge of the Self that alone brings liberation.
Action, ritual or ethical; it purifies the mind but cannot by itself bring liberation.
Liberation: the recognition of one's identity with Brahman, freedom from bondage.
Bliss; in the Taittirīya teaching, the nature of Brahman itself rather than a passing pleasure.
The witness: changeless awareness that illumines the mind and its states.
Sheath; the five layers (food, vital breath, mind, intellect, bliss) mistaken for the Self.
The three strands of nature — sattva, rajas, tamas — whose play makes up all activity.
Renunciation of action and its fruits; for Śaṅkara, closely tied to the path of knowledge.
Limiting adjunct: something that makes the limitless appear limited, like a pot enclosing space.
The Lord: Brahman seen in relation to the world, as its cause and ruler.
The individual self: consciousness identified with body and mind.
The cycle of birth and death, sustained by ignorance and action.
Dispassion: freedom from craving for the results of action, here or hereafter.
Discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, the Self and the not-Self.
The opponent's or prima facie view, stated in order to be answered.
The established conclusion, given in reply to the prima facie view.
"Not this, not this": negating every limited notion to point to Brahman.
"You are That": the great statement identifying the individual self with Brahman.
Being–consciousness–bliss: a threefold indication of Brahman's nature, not three separate attributes.
Without attributes: Brahman as it is in itself, beyond all qualities and relations.
With attributes: Brahman considered with qualities, as the Lord who creates and is worshipped.
“The fourth”: pure consciousness underlying and transcending waking, dream and deep sleep.
Apparent transformation: the world appears in Brahman without Brahman changing, as a snake appears in a rope.
Real transformation of a cause into its effect, as milk into curd; contrasted in Advaita with vivarta.
The teaching method of first attributing qualities to Brahman, then withdrawing them to reveal it.
Neither real nor simply non-existent: what appears and is later sublated, as Advaita holds of the world.
Indefinable as either real or unreal; how Advaita characterises māyā and ignorance.
Knowledge of Brahman, the subject of the Upaniṣads and the means to liberation.
Liberation while still living in the body, once knowledge has dawned.
Liberation at the fall of the body, when the karma already bearing fruit is exhausted.
One who knows Brahman; for Śaṅkara already liberated, though the body continues for a time.
Hearing the teaching of the Upaniṣads from a teacher; the first of the three disciplines of knowledge.
Reflection: removing doubts about the teaching by reasoning; the second discipline.
Contemplation: dwelling on the truth until it is unshakeable; the third discipline.
The four qualifications of a seeker: discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues, and longing for liberation.
Calmness: restraint of the mind's outgoing tendencies; first of the six virtues.
Self-restraint of the sense organs; second of the six virtues.
Withdrawal: the mind turning away from sense objects, or the giving up of ritual action.
Forbearance: enduring opposites such as heat and cold, praise and blame, without complaint.
Faith in the scriptures and the teacher's words, as the ground of understanding.
Steady concentration of the mind on the teaching; one of the six virtues.
The intense desire for liberation; the fourth qualification of a seeker.
One fitted for a teaching by preparation and disposition.
The teacher who, knowing Brahman and the scriptures, imparts the teaching.
The inner instrument: mind, intellect, ego and memory taken together.
The mind as the faculty of doubt and deliberation; part of the inner instrument.
The intellect: the deciding faculty, in which the Self's consciousness is reflected.
The ego-sense: the notion of “I” wrongly identified with body and mind.
Mind-stuff, or the faculty of memory, in the fourfold inner instrument.
Vital breath: the life-force that animates the body, often described as fivefold.
The gross body, made of the elements; the field of waking experience.
The subtle body of mind, senses and vital breaths, which passes from life to life.
The causal body: ignorance in seed form, experienced in deep sleep.
The waking state, in which the gross world is experienced.
The dream state, whose objects are projected by the mind alone.
Deep dreamless sleep, in which the mind is resolved and only ignorance and bliss remain.
A great saying of the Upaniṣads that expresses the identity of the self and Brahman.
“I am Brahman”: a great saying of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
“Consciousness is Brahman”: a great saying of the Aitareya Upaniṣad.
“This Self is Brahman”: a great saying of the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad.
“What is heard”: the Vedas and Upaniṣads, taken as revealed scripture.
“What is remembered”: traditional texts such as the Gītā, authoritative where they agree with śruti.
A means of valid knowledge, such as perception, inference and scripture.
Perception: direct knowledge through the senses.
Inference: knowledge from a sign, as of fire from smoke.
Verbal testimony, above all scripture; for Vedānta the only means of knowing Brahman.
Primal matter or nature; for Sāṅkhya the independent cause of the world, a view Śaṅkara rejects.
The Person or spirit: in Sāṅkhya a conscious principle distinct from matter, in the Upaniṣads the Self.
A latent tendency left by past experience and action, shaping desire.
An impression left in the mind by experience, the seed of memory and future tendency.
Karma that has begun to bear fruit in this life; it runs its course until the body falls, even for the knower.
Accumulated karma from past lives not yet bearing fruit; destroyed by knowledge.
Karma being done now that would bear fruit later; it does not cling to the knower.
Duty or right order; in philosophical usage also a property or attribute.
Bondage: experience as a limited, transmigrating individual, rooted in ignorance.
Aloneness or absolute freedom: the Self abiding in itself, free of all association.
Absorption: the mind wholly fixed on its object, or resolved in the Self.
Absorption without any distinction of knower, knowing and known.
Absorption in which the distinction of knower, knowing and known remains.
Identity, or the mistaken identification of the Self with what is not the Self.
Changeless as an anvil: the Self that stays unmoved amid all change.
Reflected consciousness: the Self's light appearing in the mind, like the sun in water.
Substratum: the real basis on which something is superimposed, as the rope beneath the snake.
The rope mistaken for a snake: the standard illustration of superimposition.
Empirical reality: the world as valid for practical life until Brahman is known.
The ultimate standpoint, from which Brahman alone is real.
Illusory appearance, such as dream objects or the snake seen in a rope, sublated even in ordinary experience.
Name and form: the differentiated world, apparently imposed on Brahman.
The veiling power of ignorance, which conceals the Self.
The projecting power of ignorance, which projects the world of names and forms.
Discrimination between seer and seen: consciousness is never an object.
The cosmic mind or first-born: the totality of subtle bodies.
The cosmic gross body: the totality of the gross world.
The sacred syllable, a symbol of Brahman whose parts the Māṇḍūkya relates to the states of consciousness.
Devout meditation on Brahman or a symbol; for Rāmānuja, the knowledge that leads to release.
Meditation: a steady flow of thought toward one object.
Loving devotion to the Lord; for Rāmānuja a form of meditation, for Śaṅkara a preparation for knowledge.
Play: creation as the Lord's spontaneous sport, needing no motive (Brahma Sūtra II.1.33).
One's own essential nature, as distinct from accidental attributes.
Direct, immediate realisation of the Self, not mediated by reasoning.
“End of the Veda”: the Upaniṣads and the philosophies based on them, Advaita among them.
Non-duality: the teaching that Brahman alone is real and the self is not different from it.
Qualified non-dualism, Rāmānuja's teaching: one Brahman qualified by real souls and matter.
Duality; also Madhva's school, which holds souls and world eternally distinct from God.
